content: The document is a systematic overview of reviews on comprehensive school health services (SHS), developed in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO). It outlines the methodology and findings of a systematic review of systematic reviews (SOSR) on SHS, focusing on interventions delivered by health providers in schools. The publication adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and includes a detailed protocol that defines objectives, search strategies, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and quality appraisal methods. The systematic search was conducted across databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library. The search strategy was developed with input from a librarian experienced in systematic reviews and an SHS expert. The review included studies where at least 50% of participants were school-aged children (5–19 years) and interventions were school-based or school-linked, delivered by health providers, and aimed at improving health outcomes. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled studies (NCSs), and other non-randomized intervention studies. Systematic reviews had to meet specific criteria, such as being published in peer-reviewed journals, written in English, and including the term systematic review in the title or abstract. The findings revealed that while many systematic reviews focused on mental health and oral health interventions, there were significant gaps in other health areas, such as vaccinations, communicable diseases, and injuries. No systematic reviews evaluated comprehensive SHS addressing multiple health areas. The strongest evidence supported the implementation of anxiety prevention programs, asthma education, and vision screening with free spectacles. The SOSR highlighted the need for more systematic reviews to assess routine, comprehensive SHS and their effectiveness. These reviews should evaluate the content, quality, intensity, delivery methods, and cost of SHS to guide policymakers in making evidence-based recommendations for school health services. The publication emphasizes the importance of transparency and adherence to WHO guidelines in developing and disseminating such reviews.
